title: Generating Assessments
answer: Generating assessments in course design and teaching covers the use of AI to produce questions, tasks, rubrics, and feedback prompts that align with learning outcomes. It includes formative checks, summative exams, practice sets, and alternative formats such as scenario-based items. The work sits between instructional design, subject matter expertise, and language model capability. It is not a replacement for teaching judgment but a way to draft and vary assessment materials at scale.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: Generating assessments in course design and teaching covers the use of AI to produce questions, tasks, rubrics, and feedback prompts that align with learning outcomes. It includes formative checks, summative exams, practice sets, and alternative formats such as scenario-based items. The work sits between instructional design, subject matter expertise, and language model capability. It is not a replacement for teaching judgment but a way to draft and vary assessment materials at scale.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: What it runs on: large language models accessed through APIs or embedded in learning management systems, plus retrieval over course readings, lecture notes, and prior exams. Some setups use local or hosted models, vector databases for source grounding, and templates that enforce item formats. Outputs are stored in item banks, question pools, or assessment platforms. Version control and logging matter because generated items may be revised or reused across terms.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: How the work is done: an instructor or designer writes a prompt that specifies the learning objective, cognitive level, item type, and constraints such as length or difficulty. The model generates candidate items, which are then reviewed, edited, and tagged by a human. Retrieval-augmented generation can ground items in assigned texts, and automated checks can flag duplicates, bias, or answer leakage. Iteration with student data or expert review improves alignment and clarity.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risk and provenance: generated assessments raise questions about copyright in source materials, ownership of model outputs, and the provenance of each item. Institutions need review workflows for accuracy, fairness, accessibility, and alignment with accommodation policies. Student data used for calibration or personalization must be handled under privacy rules, and item banks should record which model, prompt, and source produced each question. Transparency with students about AI involvement is part of responsible practice.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: Where it is going: expect tighter integration with learning platforms, adaptive testing, and real-time generation of practice items from course content. Research on validity, bias, and item quality will shape standards for when generated assessments are acceptable. The field is moving toward human-AI co-design, where instructors set the blueprint and models handle drafting and variation. Evaluation will focus on learning outcomes, not on the volume of items produced.
